subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
Although three or four hon. members on this side of the chamber adopted the attitude of sitting on their hands, I am sure that the general applause will strengthen for today the position of unification for the Minister of National Defence.
I would like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. For several weeks I have been trying to get information on the attitude by Canada with reference to the two-China proposition. Indeed I have placed before the house by questions what I have known only through the press, but as yet we have not been able to secure anything in the nature of information, though the press is full of it.
I ask the minister, now that the debate is under way or will be under way today in the United Nations, will he tell parliament what the Canadian government intends to do rather than have us wait until a statement is made in the United Nations?
Second, will he assure the Canadian people that whatever is done by the United Nations resolution, which apparently has been joined in by Italy, Chile and Canada, it will not in any way sacrifice the government of the Republic of China that has stood for freedom through dark years and, above all, that the people there will not be a sacrifice to the Red Guards who are running rampant today?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my absence the Prime Minister dealt with questions not unlike those which have just been put by the right hon. gentleman. As he said, the story in the press was speculative, and the story which I saw this morning is also speculative. We are, however, having consultations with a number of countries designed to see if we cannot provide a solution to a problem that has dogged the United Nations for some time.
These consultations are continuing. I had some myself in Rome on Monday. They are now continuing in New York. I will be going to the United Nations. I cannot of course indicate what will be the outcome of these consultations. I can say to the right hon. gentlemen that it is not the intention of the government of Canada in any way to encourage the expulsion from the United Nations of the government of Formosa. It is, however, our intention to do all we can to see that an effort is made to reach the principle of universality in the United Nations.
At any rate we have already declared our policy.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: When?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: On September 27 I stated that the government would like to see the People's Republic of China take its place in the United Nations organization, but we would not agree to that happening at the expense of another government. That would be a denial of the principle of universality.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is a long way from an answer. Why should not this parliament know the kind of proposition that the minister and those associated with him are advancing in the United Nations? Why are we denied what the press in the United States and elsewhere throughout the world is able to secure? What is the nature of this plan that the minister has in mind? Why hide it from parliament and deny us the opportunity to discuss it before it is revealed officially, as it has already been revealed unofficially, to all the press that is represented in New York?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I told my right hon. friend that the story was speculative. There has been no revelation to any news media whatever.
I do not want to enter into a controversy with my right hon. friend today on his return to the house, but he knows, as an experienced parliamentarian, that the conduct of the policy of the government in foreign affairs is a matter that the executive determines. Once a position has been taken, it is open to parliament to take issue with that policy. Foreign policy cannot be pursued in any other way. We are pursuing the same method which my right hon. friend, and all governments under our system, have pursued. We have stated the principles-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: You do not have a bipartisan policy when you hide it from the house.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be controversial with my right hon. friend on this very first day. I am trying to respect-

speechtext: He never left the house.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: I am trying to respect my right hon. friend's return to the house, and I want him to know I have made-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
We know what you meant.
November 18, 1968

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: Well, I just want to say to the Prime Minister-to the right hon. gentleman-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that I should give that kind of comfort to my right hon. friend. What I was trying to say to him, as one who has been in politics and a member of this house for a long time, was that I, along with the Prime Minister and others, join in welcoming him back today. In the circumstances I would have hoped that he and those sitting behind him would have recognized the sporting quality of our joining in that welcome.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I always admire the sporting quality of the hon. gentleman, but what we are talking about today is not sport but the future of mankind. Why should not parliament know what this government has decided? Why should we wait until a speech is made in the United Nations before we can determine whether it is a proper one? As far as the executive having the responsibility for foreign affairs, is concerned, I thought our attitude in this country was that both major parties and the other parties should reasonably agree with our foreign policy, rather than its becoming the monopoly of the government.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Could the Secretary of State for External Affairs tell the house whether, in the opinion of the government, a two-China policy holds out any hope whatever, when apparently it is rejected both by the People's Republic of China and the so-called nationalist government of China? Could he say whether or not as a result of the matters discussed in the talks he mentioned a proposal is being put forward that the People's Republic of China should be recognized and accepted within the United Nations as the representative of China, and that the other regime might be recognized and accepted as the government of Taiwan, where I understand it does in fact have control?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that question is an argumentative one. We have, of course, stated our position, which is that while we believe that no sovereign body should be precluded from participating in the United Nations, we do not agree to take that position at the expense of another country that is entitled to membership in the organization.
Inquiries of the Ministry We are having consultations and we are discussing this matter with other countries. Until those consultations have been completed it is not possible for me to go any further.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: A further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the minister's remarks on the admission of the People's Republic of China to the United Nations, is the government now planning to give diplomatic recognition to the People's Republic of China in light of the fact that we have now initiated trading programs with China amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION REGARDING ADMISSION OF MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question of the recognition of the regime diplomatically in one form or another or through some other process, is a matter which has not been involved in the questions which have been put this morning. This is a question that stands by itself, and the government's policy in this regard will be announced to the house in due course.

Mr. Chairman, there are a few things I should like to say, if the committee feels like devoting the time to my remarks at this late stage of our consideration of estimates. In May when the officials of the department and I appeared before the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, I reviewed the activities of the various branches of the Department of Trade and Commerce in some detail. We had good discussions centering around our export trade policies and promotion techniques, and we examined in considerable detail the program represented by the estimates now before the house.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
I was gratified to note the committee's approval of a continuing high level of activity by Canada's trade commissioner service to stimulate external trade, and the recommendation to the branches of the department to continue an aggressive program of export promotion. One step to broaden the various aspects of our trade commissioner service is that we are now doing more to encourage young ladies to apply. I am hopeful that suitable qualified candidates will come forward for recruitment.
The importance of our export trade to the national economy is well recognized. Having in mind the total area of export trade promotion and policy development, it is a major concern of the department to deploy the staff and financial resources available to it in accordance with priorities which recognize the constantly shifting trade patterns and trading relationships, as well as varying supply and demand factors. It is our aim to neglect no part of our economy where we find capacity to export. We are, however, paying particular attention to foreign markets where the potential return is high. Our greatest effort is expended where we get best value in export terms for the expenditures incurred.
Exports to date in 1966 are up 20 per cent from the same period a year ago, to a new high in Canada's export performance. Merchandise exports for 1966 as a whole are likely to reach or even exceed the $10 billion
November 18, 1966

Supply-Trade and Commerce events of our centennial year, which I am convinced will be a great success.
Mr. Chairman, I want to refer to two other developments related to our commodities. As hon. members know, during the year we found it necessary to take control of copper in certain forms, and control re-exports of hides and skins. We did this in the latter case because the United States government took control of hides and skins but allowed them to come into Canada on the understanding that we in turn would prevent the re-export of hides and skins coming into Canada from the United States. The United States authorities have lifted their embargo on hides and skins, and accordingly we have done the same for re-export. They are now free for export. That action was taken by our government just a few days ago.
On the matter of copper ores and concentrates, we had to take a certain measure of control. This applied to scrap as well, except for those grades which were not satisfactory for use in Canada. The situation has eased somewhat. The Canadian demand and supply picture looks to be relatively more in balance. We are now permitting the export of copper scrap on a quota basis. We have not interfered at all with the export of copper concentrates from the west coast because there are no readily accessible smelters. In the east we have found it possible to allow certain mines to export their concentrates. We intend to review these permits as they come up for renewal from time to time; but we feel that more leniency in granting export permits on an annual basis, than is currently the case, vill become possible.

Mr. Chairman, as a member of the finance committee I simply want to say that we examined the estimates of this department in considerable detail and the committee made a report to which I would draw the attention of all hon. members. I should like to make one or two minor remarks in connection with this department.
First of all, with regard to the negotiations for the reduction of tariffs under what is familiarly known as the Kennedy round, although this matter does not come directly under the minister's jurisdiction I am sure he is involved in it. His colleague the Minister of Finance, through the tariff section, is more directly involved in this question. The chemical producers of Canada have put forward, in my view, a very strong and justifiable case that no unilateral decision should be taken by

the government to instruct Canada's negotiating team to arrive at certain levels of tariffs with regard to chemicals produced commercially in Canada, without direct consultation with the industry. This is vital to the Canadian industry.
I am sure that if the minister has seen the brief of the association or has talked to members of the association he will readily understand how the whole of the Canadian chemical industry could, frankly, be torpedoed by improper action on the part of our government; that is, if the government were instructing their negotiators to set certain levels at which they would be prepared to deal.
These are the only remarks I wish to make on this occasion, Mr. Chairman, because the committee has examined these estimates in detail. We will certainly be interested to see the progress that is made by Canada in reducing the extraordinarily large imbalance of trade with the United States on commodity account, and also the progress that is made in regard to our own deficit on commodity account.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Having said this, generally speaking I think we may let the estimates pass although I and my colleagues may have some questions to ask.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver East.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry for the delay in getting to my feet but unfortunately I am somewhat disabled physically. I am most anxious however to speak on certain matters which fall under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I noted that the minister said-and I quote him because I took his words down

that the value of export trade is nationally recognized. I agree with that; but export trade by Canada entails an understanding that if we want to expand it we must also give consideration to imports. If my understanding of economics is correct, and I believe it is, we have to recognize, with respect to trade deficiencies, that the more we bring together exports and imports the greater is our opportunity for exports.
My reason for participating in this debate under these difficult circumstances is to say regretfully that I have had to reach a conclusion that the Liberal government is so much interested in giving advantage to United States exports into Canada that it is betraying, and I repeat betraying, opportunities for
November 18, 1966

greater exports from the United Kingdom to Canada.
We have a deficiency situation as between Canada and the United States, with Canada being on the wrong side of the ledger. The United Kingdom, on the other hand, has a deficiency of payments problem with Canada, and it is my belief it should be government policy to reduce that deficiency in trade balance between the United Kingdom and Canada. The more we can import from the United Kingdom the greater will be our exports to the United Kingdom. Therefore I am most disturbed when I find the Canadian government policy giving advantage to the United States to export to Canada, and in some respects denying the right to the United Kingdom to export to Canada.
I had the opportunity and privilege of spending the first week of July last in Sheffield, England, and while there visited some of the local major steel industries. I met with members of parliament and councillors who have the same philosophical belief as myself, but I also met with some of the top industrial leaders. I was taken through two of the largest steel industries in Sheffield by a couple of those industrial leaders, one the president and the other the managing director. They told me they were most happy because just that day they had received a second large order from the United States automotive industry for automotive steel. Naturally I asked them, "What automotive steel do you send to Canada, because we have a large automotive industry"? Their answer was that none is sent here. I then asked, "Why do you not sell to Canada?" Their answer was "Because your government made an automotive agreement with the United States whereby we in the United Kingdom cannot sell automotive steel to Canada." I queried this and their answer was "We can and we will supply automotive steel to Canada at between 12 per cent and 15 per cent less than our selling price to the United States, less even than the price involved in the second big contract we have now got from the Ford Motor Company in the Unites States, but your Canadian government, by its automotive agreement, has made it impossible for us to sell anything to the automotive industry in Canada."
I see the Minister of Trade and Commerce shaking his head, but I tell him this information was given to me directly in Sheffield by men who certainly should know the situation. When the U.S.-Canada automobile agreement
Supply-Trade and Commerce came before this house I am sure not one of us realized that that was the situation-that the United Kingdom could not sell automotive steel to the industry in Canada.
Again I tell the minister, who knows parliament, who knows trade administration and, though he was not here for some time, was involved in finance and big industry, that this was the information given to me in Sheffield by two top men in the steel industry. I believe I have not only the right but the responsibility to ask the minister to give some explanation about this situation, and if the situation is as I have described it, then he should explain this betrayal of the United Kingdom in this matter.
There are other factors I wish to mention. Admittedly they come under revenue and customs, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce has a major interest in trade and if the steel industry in the United Kingdom cannot get anywhere with our revenue and customs restrictions, perhaps the minister could do something about the matter.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
Let me refer again to the talks I had during my visit to Sheffield, the home of highly specialized steel interests. I spoke to the president-at his request because he was interested in Canadian trade-of a firm which is almost two centuries old. It specializes in the manufacture of agricultural machinery parts, files saws, scythes, etc. He does little business with Canada and I asked him why. He said: "Because your parliament and your government prefer to give the United States the right to export to Canada a privilege not extended to us from the United Kingdom". I asked him whether he would put this in writing and he did, and I have the correspondence before me lest I be challenged on it.
What is the situation, Mr. Chairman? As far as I know and as far as these people in the United Kingdom know there is only one company in Canada which manufactures high-class specialized steel for machinery parts, saws, scythes, etc., and they manufacture these parts for their own use. Other companies which require farm machinery and related parts import them from the United States.
They do this, Mr. Chairman, because of government regulation. Manufacturers in the United States are able to quote one price for the year. Their freight charges are such that they can quote a yearly price. Exports from the United Kingdom are shipped via the seaway while the seaway is open, but when it
10056	COMMONS
Supply-Trade and Commerce closes these goods have to be landed at Saint John and then go by rail. The companies in Canada who are prepared to buy this steel cutting equipment insist upon a price for the year because their business is operated on a computer basis. They require a guaranteed price for the year, and the United States can meet this requirement because freight charges there do not change during the year., The representatives of the two companies I spoke to in Sheffield say that they would be prepared to give a one year guaranteed price to meet Canadian requirements and would take a chance on whether the seaway would be open, carrying the loss incurred by landing at Saint John and then shipping by rail when the seaway is closed.
This is something, Mr. Chairman, which the government will not allow. The government insist on an f.o.b. price Manchester or Liverpool, plus freight charges at the time of shipment. Because of this regulation of the government, specialized steel products from the United Kingdom cannot be shipped on a one year guaranteed price basis, in order thereby to meet United States competition, that can offer this one year guaranteed price. To me it is an irresponsible and an unfair government regulation which would deny the United Kingdom the right to bid on a one year price basis.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, I have the correspondence from these industrialists in Sheffield before me, but I am not going to read it. However, I would say, Mr. Chairman, that I do not think it is understood by many backbenchers in this house that there is a government regulation which gives United States steel manufacturers top priority to sell their products to Canada while at the same time denying the United Kingdom, which has a big trade deficit with Canada, any opportunity of selling steel products to Canada.
I sincerely hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will take note of what I am saying, Mr. Chairman, and that he will have the decency and honesty to explain why automotive steel cannot be sold in Canada, despite the fact, as I was told by the president of this steel complex in the United Kingdom, that the price could be 12 to 15 per cent less than that of steel being sold to the Ford Motor Company of the United States. I should also like to know why, when only one company in Canada produces high grade agricultural machinery for its own use, government regulation is such that the United Kingdom is

DEBATES	November 18, 1966
unable to bid for what Canadian companies demand, namely a one year price, thereby handing on a silver platter to the United States this Canadian business.
I agree with what the minister said not too long ago about the value to Canada of exports. But Canadian exports could increase even faster if some consideration were to be given to the balance which exists between our imports and our exports. I, as one who thought he knew about government regulations, was amazed and disturbed at the information given me in Sheffield by those who should know, those who are employed in the industrial steel empire of the United Kingdom, information which indicates that there are government regulations which deny the United Kingdom the opportunity of exporting to its greatest Commonwealth colleague, the Dominion of Canada.
I sincerely hope that the minister will give me an explanation of this and that some study will be made of this most important matter. I certainly hope the minister will not try to give me any eyewash, or the brushoff, because what I have been telling him about during the past few minutes is based on information given me by industrial leaders in Sheffield, who I would think should know the regulations relating to export and import. I will look forward to hearing from the Minister of Trade and Commerce on what I consider to be two mighty important matters, about which I can assure him I did not know until they were drawn to my attention by the political and industrial leaders of the United Kingdom.

Mr. Chairman, I should just like to comment on the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver East, but before I do so I should like as a matter of record to reply to what the hon. member for Edmonton West had to say about consulting the chemical industry on any change in the tariff structure. I should like to inform the members of the committee that consultation is taking place in this regard. We have had very close consultation with many branches of industry in these tariff negotiations. The views of this industry have been received. They are being taken into account by the government in determining its position on the matter of chemicals raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
Referring to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East, which are always made vigorously and dynamically, and which are well documented, I would say there is always room for both understanding and
November 18, 1966	COMMONS
misunderstanding. My interest in getting our trade into a better balance with the United Kingdom is as great as anybody's. Since I have had this portfolio, and before, steps have been taken to make it easier for United Kingdom exporters to trade in Canada. That those steps are effective is revealed by the figures. In September, 1966, Canadian exports to the United Kingdom dropped, whereas imports from the United Kingdom to Canada have gone up from $90.2 million to $95.6 million. United Kingdom exports to Canada increased by 13.1 per cent over September 1965. We have taken various steps to help them meet valuation difficulties which they feel have been plaguing them to a considerable extent.
Officials from the government have been in the Un ted Kingdom discussing these problems, a number of which have been isolated and solved to make it still easier for the United Kingdom to trade here.
To allow us to examine problems at first hand on a periodic basis, the United Kingdom government acted on the strength of a suggestion the government of Canada made to them at the time of the Trade Ministers Conference in the United Kingdom earlier this year. We suggested to them that they avail themselves of the same opportunities the United States now has through the medium of a joint ministerial committee. The United Kingdom accepted the suggestion. We are thus setting up a joint ministerial committee which undoubtedly will give its major emphasis to matters of trade. But it is open to them to bring up what they wish. The first meeting will be held shortly after the turn of the year.
I hope the achievements of that committee will be substantial and that it will eliminate a great deal of current misunderstanding.
In the specific field of specialty steels, the hon. member undoubtedly knows that in this country we produce excellent specialty steels at competitive prices. Now that the automobile agreement has come into effect we have access, if we can achieve it on the basis of price, quality, delivery and the other elements in trade, to the whole North American automotive market. Part of the problem involves the Canadian content of cars. The Canadian content provision was imposed by the government of Canada to ensure the maximum work effort and maximum value added to the Canadian cars. But there is no bar that [ know of to the importation into this country of United Kingdom stainless or specialty steels. To my knowledge British stainless
23033-637 J
Supply-Trade and Commerce steels are imported into Canada now and have use and application here. There is no special exclusion. If they can meet us on terms of price, delivery and all the other elements going into the trading pattern, the Canadian market is available to them, and in fact it is available to them now.
I wish to follow up the specific instances the hon. member brought to my attention. I should like our people to communicate directly, with the distinguished gentlemen concerned, to see if we cannot eliminate any misunderstanding, and to solve directly any d.fficulties which may arise. It is our aim to reduce barriers to trade on a multilateral basis, but if I may particularlize with one country specifically, we want to see a better trade balance between the United Kingdom and Canada.

The minister is evading the question I asked him. He referred to stainless steel, but at no time did I refer to stainless steel. I referred to cutting steel. My information is that Massey-Ferguson Industries Limited produce cutting steel only for themselves. I understand the United Kingdom must quote two prices, whereas the United States manufacturers quote only one. Does the minister not think that is damnably unfair to the cutting steel industry of the United Kingdom?

Mr. Chairman, I referred to stainless steels and other specialty steels. My argument about stainless steels applies equally to specialty steels of all kinds. I wish to look at the particular instance the hon. member brought to my attention, because we might be helpful. I want to be as helpful as possible.
That is all that I am asking. I ask that you be helpful to the United Kingdom.

I am not a member of the standing committee to which the estimates of this department were referred. I realize that these estimates have been considered in detail by that committee and returned to the house. I do not intend to take much time to discuss them because I wish to refer to only two matters at this time.
I do not know if I should congratulate the minister for being assigned the responsibility for the Canadian Wheat Board, but I do wish him well. Congratulations imply achievement. The wheat board may be a burden under the present circumstances.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
When the Minister of Finance was responsible for the wheat board there was discussion about the working out of a new quota system for the delivery of grain from the producers to the elevator companies in the areas serviced by the wheat board. The Minister of Finance never told the house the details of plans for setting up new quota systems for wheat deliveries. I realize that from time to time there have been difficulties in the system, and we want to know what the department or what the wheat board is doing to correct some of the inadequacies and weaknesses found in the present quota system. For example, we know there are wide discrepancies in quotas at various points. I do not know whether some points have no quotas, but some points a few days ago were not up to even a one bushel quota. I realize there are many shipping points in western Canada, but I also realize that some places have a quota of between five and six bushels per acre at the present time.
You can try to explain these discrepancies to the farmers by saying that it is necessary for the greatest amount of grain to get into export position by taking in the short hauls first before the St. Lawrence freezes, and so on. But no matter how you try to explain this, you still run into a situation such as I have in my constituency where, on a Canadian Pacific line running from Bassano to Empress, for example, almost all points are on a one or two bushel quota.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
Only 50 or 60 miles north, where the C.N.R. runs through, most of these points are now on a quota of four or five bushels per acre. The difference in the quota along these two railway lines cannot be explained away; it does not accord with the explanation that the railways are required to move short haul grain to the lakehead before the lakes are closed. I hope some other arrangement can be worked out so that there may be more equal application of the quota system, including the dates when these quotas are open. There is no good and satisfactory reason for the present wide differences. I make a plea to the minister to do whatever he can in full co-operation with the wheat board, the railway companies and the elevator companies to make sure that this disparity in quotas is not repeated year after year.
This is not a new thing. It happened last year, and it happened the year before that. For farmers who are able to sell only one or

two bushels per acre by the end of the calendar year while others not far away are able to sell three or four times as much, the system is not satisfactory, and no satisfactory explanation can be given to them.
Discussions have been taking place, either in the minister's department or in the Department of Transport, about the possibility of providing new equipment for railways. I refer in particular to special equipment for the hauling of grain. It seems to me that general purpose box cars which need to be fitted with grain doors and papered up before they can be used for the transport of grain are not satisfactory, in the light of present conditions, and that other types of hopper cars could be designed to carry grain more efficiently. I am thinking of cars designed so as to minimize time spent loading and unloading; cars which would, in any case, be able to carry much larger quantities of grain.
It seems to me we should recognize that the potential production of wheat in western Canada has increased substantially in the last few years, not only because of the increase in the number of acres under cultivation but also because of new methods, fertilizers and so on. Along with this has come a reasonably assured increase in the prospects of the sale of our wheat on international markets.
We have been accustomed to export a volume of wheat in the neighbourhood of 400 million bushels annually. This figure is now increasing substantially and the narrowest bottleneck encountered at the moment is failure to move our grain fast enough by rail. There were suggestions that some of the trouble was at the terminal elevators, but what little investigation I have been able to do at various times indicates that the terminal elevators are not at the present time the major limiting factor. I believe it is the responsibility of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to do something about increasing terminal space and encouraging those concerned to improve the grain handling facilities at terminal points and other export points. As I said at the outset, I wish the minister well. I hope he realizes that our production potential and the marketability of our grain have increased substantially during the past four or five years, and that the need at the present time is to provide improved facilities so as to profit from our opportunities.

targets in keeping with the potential production of oil in Canada. Those targets have not been met. Yet the production of oil has increased in every single year since then-I am referring to 1959, or 1960. Oil production in Alberta today is far below the capacity of the wells to produce even within the limits of good conservation practices. Yet we are still importing oil and petroleum products. This is a paradox, particularly when one considers that the importation of petroleum and petroleum products into Canada is one of the heaviest factors contributing to our balance of payment problem. Supply-Trade and Commerce been forced, because of foreign competition, to close down and cease production.
Cities are involved in this situation, and this creates many disadvantages for Canadian industry, and more particularly for local industry, and the fact that certain plants must close down results in loss of employment for those individuals who, until then, earned their living by working in these plants. Very important information may be found in the third supplementary brief that I have here. On the other hand, imports have risen from 2,623,000 pair in 1951, to 27,394,000 in 1965. We can see that foreign shoe imports have risen at a greater rate than Canadian production and, needless to say, such a state of affairs is detrimental to Canadian manufacturers.
Comparatively, our exports, which totalled 2,384,675 pair of shoes in 1962, fell to 1,749,461 in 1965.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief in my remarks. I want to endorse-I sometimes think I am getting too mellow these days-the remarks of the hon. member for Medicine Hat with reference to agriculture and the petroleum industry. I want to add a few words to those of the hon. member in congratulating the minister upon getting the wheat board under the Department of Trade and Commerce. I have always been one of those who believed it should really be under the Department of Agriculture; but I do not think it really matters as long as you have a good man looking after it.
Hear, hear.

I have known the Minister of Trade and Commerce for some years. I have heard him speak to the chamber of commerce in Calgary. I say without any hesitation that he is quite a gracious gentleman; I know he has the know-how with regard to many things, and it will not take him long to grasp the problems I hope of the wheat board.
As I have said, the minister spoke to the chamber of commerce in the city of Calgary, and I hope that in the months ahead he will find time to speak to the U.F.O., the farm organizations of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I also hope he will speak to the chambers of commerce in the smaller areas. I believe it is sometimes necessary for all of us in this house, particularly cabinet members, to get back to the real grass roots. It may be a good thing if the minister visited some of the small towns in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, leaned against the wall of a country store or the post office and just talked to the farmers.
There has always been the fiction that the western farmer-I know the minister will not be guilty of believing this because he has knowledge of the whole of Canada,-is rolling in money, goes to Florida in the winter and drives a big car. This is complete fiction. There are a few farmers who do this, as there are a few people in any industry who do it; but it is the exception rather than the rule.
With regard to the wheat board, I hope the minister will obtain the co-operation of his cabinet colleagues to improve the movement of grain. I believe we all know that cabinet discussions are rather like those in the House of Commons, except that the press are not present, and you have to sell ideas to your colleagues. I hope that since the Liberal party is not represented in the west, and certainly it is not at the present time, the minister will put forward his arguments forcibly in cabinet on behalf of the western farmer.
Agriculture is not a small business today; it is not the small business in which our relatives engaged some years ago. It is big business now. In order to engage in wheat farming, it is necessary in the initial stages to have anywhere from $50,000 to $100,000 worth of machinery and land comparable in value to that amount of investment.
Over the past few years the costs of farming have been gradually increasing, as have the costs in every industry in the country. The big operators of today are still able to produce grain at a profit. But we must consider the middleman, because we do not want to
November 18. 1966	COMMONS
see the west owned by a few people. If this were to be the case, the west would become a series of great grain belts in the sense that just one or two operators would be in control and would own all the communities. We want to keep small communities and towns that are dependent upon this industry. We do not want to have a monopoly situation in this industry.
When we talk about the grain industry, we are talking of a $2 billion industry. The problem is that everybody in Canada who is not from the west thinks he understands the situation. A few years ago if the grain crop ran 50 bushels to the acre, or anywhere from 25 bushels to 50 bushels to the acre, it was a good crop and there was no problem. But the problem in the agricultural industry, as in the automobile industry, is that you have to sell the commodity you are producing.
It may be that on paper the grain is sold. The markets are there, if the grain can be moved off the farms to the ports of shipment. The cash advances program introduced in 1957 was badly needed at that time because in many cases the farmer found it difficult to obtain the cash needed to buy farm machinery and pay his expenses. The wheat quotas are still very low.
A great deal of mail arrives over my desk from my constituents. The amount of mail I receive is typical of that received by western members, except that half of my constituency is city and half is rural, so that there is a division between urban and rural problems. Most of the mail I receive comes from country elevator agents and farmers who point out that they can get the grain to the elevators but the difficulty is in moving it out of the elevators to the terminals and ports from which it will be shipped to the countries which have purchased it.
Some people think I have been too critical of the C.P.R. I have said over and over again in this chamber that I believe in free enterprise, and I think the C.P.R. has been a great company. But somehow, whether it has been the fault of governments or the company, the C.P.R. is years behind in respect of the movement of grain. As the hon. member for Medicine Hat pointed out, the company is years behind in automating its equipment. It is not easy to do this, and it is a very expensive matter. When the C.P.R. changed from steam to diesel locomotives, the cost ran into millions of dollars. No doubt it will cost millions of dollars for them to automate the facilities at the terminals. However, Mr. Chairman, I still believe that one of the big
Supply-Trade and Commerce problems in this area, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat mentioned, is the inability to obtain sufficient cars to move the grain. The big problem today seems to be in the hold-up of cars.
I am told over and over again that 10, 15 or 20 cars will back into a siding but nothing happens. Therefore, I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with the co-operation of the Minister of Transport, will consult the officials of the railway and get these box cars moving to the port of shipment, whether it be Vancouver, Port Arthur or Fort William. At these ports there is a hold-up of box car movements because the railways are not automated.
If any industry in Canada as big as the grain industry were completely under free enterprise, these problems would not arise. The movement of grain is under the control of the wheat board, an agency of the government. I am confident that any other industry of this size would be fully automated in a very short time in order to compete. These problems arise because of government control and regulation. I support the wheat board because it organizes the seller as well as the purchaser of wheat, so that we have over the years obtained a fair return for our grain.
After the minister has obtained the facts at the grass roots, I ask him to talk to the railroad people, as well as others concerned, and convince them that something must be done to improve this situation. It must be done immediately. If the railroads keep the equipment they have, then something must be done to move the grain as quickly as possible so that the grain Canada has sold can be delivered.
I suppose that every government likes to hide a few facts. I am sure we did it when our party formed the government, and I am sure the Liberals do it now they are the government. However, Mr. Chairman, we want to get down to brass tacks. On several occasions, I have pressed the Minister of Finance to answer questions I have put to him as to whether we lost grain sales last year because of delays in delivery caused by railway strikes, longshoremen's strikes and other problems. Mr. McNamara, head of the wheat board, said that irreparable damage had been done to our grain markets. I know that in cabinet discussions the minister can raise these matters with his colleagues; but at other times one has to be careful about the words one uses. I do not care whether you are Liberal, Conservative,
November 18. 1966

Supply-Trade and Commerce Social Credit or N.D.P., when you are speaking before the public about any matter you must be a little careful about the words used.
[DOT] (1:20 p.m.)
This is a serious economic problem and I tell the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he could build a great image for himself in western Canada if he really did something about it. Over the years that I have been in this chamber I have heard successive ministers say they were going to give it serious consideration, but that means nothing. The consideration which the average man thinks about as worthwhile results in something really happening.
We have lost some of our markets because of the delay. When you have a two bushel or a three bushel quota, and you have to build bins to store the grain which you cannot sell, this *creates difficulty. I do not say the difficulty is rampant. I do not want to exaggerate, but there were cases where trucks were being repossessed during a time of prosperity simply because the farmers could not make delivery of their grain. In most cases the people involved were those who recently got into the industry and did not have that backlog of capital built up over the years as did those whose pioneering fathers settled on the farms.
When I was a boy on a wheat farm, before I left home and became a lawyer, I remember the complaint heard at breakfast, dinner and supper, was that we could not sell the wheat. Drought has never hurt Saskatchewan as much or as badly as low prices. I remember when wheat was 23 cents a bushel. I remember in one instance in 1930 1,000 pounds of beef were shipped from Rosetown to Winnipeg, and after the freight costs were deducted my father got only 16 cents for the whole 1,000 lb. beast.
The situation now is that we have a market but we cannot make deliveries. I say, let us get the product moving. I am not particularly criticising the Minister of Trade and Commerce because he has just taken over responsibility for the wheat board, but I say to him that he can build an image for himself in western Canada if he tackles this problem .and provides the solution. I beg him to do that. I ask the minister to go out and do what I suggest.
I know the minister wants to help because I heard him speak to the Chamber of Commerce in Calgary, and I thought he had a great appreciation not only of the grain trade but of the petroleum industry. I say to him, go and talk to these people. Give them some confidence, and after that do a job for them.

I made what I felt was a major address during the interim supply debate on the petroleum industry and the Trans-Canada pipe lines project. I am not going to reopen that argument now, because if too much is said it will harm the company's application before the Federal Power Commission in the United States. At present powerful lobbies are working in the United States to keep Canadian products out of the United States market. But that is normal. I am not opposed to the Americans doing this. As a Canadian I can appreciate their lobbying against our products, but I do not fear lobbies. Today they are a part of influence in the business world and the political world. I do not blame anybody for trying to use this issue to win a few electoral seats in a certain area of the country, but I think we should consider the Canadian interests as a whole.
The National Energy Board is chaired by an Albertan, a man who has spent practically his whole fife in the petroleum industry, and who has served on the conservation board. He is working with his experts and has the advantage of the rules of law laid down in the National Energy Board Act. He is doing a good job in taking care of Canada's interests. Trans-Canda's second application was approved by that board, and by the government. I believe they were absolutely right to do so, and time will prove them to have been right. But, as I say, the problem is that every time one makes a comment on this matter-and I may be guilty of this too-it does irreparable harm to the company in the hearings being held by the federal commission in the United States.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat quite properly said that our petroleum exports to the United States are on a quote basis. When we got into difficulty after the Suez crisis was over, our domestic and export markets decreased by 200,000 to 300,000 barrels of crude oil per day. But a former minister of trade and commerce, the hon. member from Winnipeg South Centre, and the hon. member for Northumberland made a deal with the United States which permitted us entry into the western United States market. In return we permitted them to have the eastern Canadian market. This was a mutually beneficial agreement because it is cheaper to ship our petroleum into the western States than to bring it to eastern Canada. It is likewise cheaper for the United States to ship petroleum to eastern Canada.

We cannot isolate ourselves in present day economics. People who call themselves nationalists and who say Canada first, who say we must keep everything within our borders, are preaching an outdated philosophy. We are becoming highly industrialized. We have got energy that we can afford to export because it is in surplus quantity, but we must make certain that its cost is kept in balance with United States costs so that we may benefit Canada's interests.
When we attack this program, particularly in view of the sensitivity of that industry, we are attacking ourselves. If the petroleum and grain industries of western Canada fail, their failure will affect our whole economy. They are our greatest aids in balancing our trade with the United States, and surely everyone should appreciate this. In that regard, I endorse the government's stand 100 per cent, but again I urge the minister to go to Calgary and speak with representatives of the petroleum industry. He should learn their problems, learn about the grass roots of the industry, and then devote his energies to making certain that our export targets climb year by year.
When a drilling rig is idle in Alberta or Saskatchewan, who suffers? It is not only management but labour, and everyone all down the line. I say to my good friends in the N.D.P. who represent labour interests-and of course labour interests must have a voice- they must realize that if they kill this industry they kill thousands of jobs in Canada. There has to be a balance.
I could cite as an example the coal industry in western Canada. We used to see six or seven mines operating in the Drumheller valley, but now there is only one still struggling to keep open. Men are living in poverty in this country of ours which is experiencing prosperity. Only when capital and management are flourishing can labour earn a decent living.
I have talked longer than I intended to, Mr. Chairman, but I hope the minister will take some of the things I have said to heart. He can build a great image and a great future not only for himself but for Canada if he does what I suggest.

If Canada develops, as undoubtedly it will, there is no question but that the ports on the eastern coast will advance also in volume of exports and imports handled. But having said that, Mr. Chairman, I wish to state that it cannot be challenged that in the years ahead the major advance in Canada's
Supply-Trade and Commerce trade is going to be over the Pacific. The U.S.S.R. will be importing more than wheat from us, and the route will be over the Pacific because on the Atlantic coast the U.S.S.R. has only one port, a small one, that is open for 12 months a year. Opposite the Pacific coast we have China, Japan and Australasia, and there will be major advances in trade over the Pacific. No doubt the Minister of Trade and Commerce is already working on that.

In working to advance our export and import trade, we also require the necessary facilities. In this connection, I am not just referring to wheat or grain; I am referring to facilities to handle bulk commodity shipments, especially on the Pacific side where we now have ships with a capacity of 175,000 tons calling at ports. In fact, I read only last week of two contracts let for the construction of ships of 225,000 tons capacity.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, when we think of trade we must think not only of the goals that the Minister of Trade and Commerce may have in mind, but also of the facilities required to handle an increasing volume of imports and exports.
Along with this we must also consider competition. Here, I refer to the position on the Pacific coast. Vancouver and New Westminster in particular are very close to the ports of Portland, Seattle and San Francisco. In 1924 the government of the day built the Ballan-tyne pier. In fact, I worked on that pier as an apprentice electrician. The government at that time imposed a charge of three cents per ton for the use of the port facilities in order to pay for the Ballantyne pier. The pier has been paid off mere than once already, this three cents per ton is still being imposed.
The Pacific ports of Vancouver, New Westminster, Victoria and Prince Rupert should be able to look forward to an unchallenged future, but because it takes three, four or five years to build port facilities, and because of this extra charge in the port of Vancouver, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who I know is sincere in his position, must realize that selling goods is not enough. We must have the required facilities on the Pacific coast. Vancouver and British Columbia have had promises galore from both Liberal and Conservative governments in the past, but unfortunately in the main all they have had has been promises. If they were not given promises, they were told the matter was under consideration.

Only recently in Vancouver, the Minister of Transport had a great deal to say about the future, but he said nothing specific. I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce this question: I presume he must be in contact with the departments of revenue and transport, and must be familiar with harbour charges and customs.
