Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East I think I should say that the questions he posed fall within the jurisdiction of a number of my colleagues, who perhaps would prefer to answer for themselves. However, we are well
fMr. Winch.]
aware of the requirements for keeping pace with shipping developments. I myself have been following with interest the development of enormous freighters of over 200,000 tons, which itself is a great feat. I know they have been used in the iron ore industry and elsewhere to great advantage, and the facilities at our shipping terminals must also develop in commensurate manner.
To that end, the hon. member may recall that last week the Minister of Transport announced an extension of the boundaries of Vancouver harbour to include Sturgeon Bank, Roverts Bank and Boundary Bay, which are all outside Vancouver harbour. At the time he stated the national harbours board will accept responsibility for facilities demanded in the future by ships of deeper draught in order that the new commodities may be moved.
At the same time, I should remind the hon. member that there is more than one ice-free port on the Atlantic coast, as the hon. members for Halifax will be so ready to inform him. There is also Saint John-
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but what I said was ice-free port in the U.S.S.R. on the Atlantic side. There is only one, the others are on the Pacific coast.
I do not think the hon. member will mind me reminding him that there are good ice-free ports on the Atlantic coast of Canada, too.
They are not little ones, either.

Yes, other than little ones.
With regard to the Russian contract, as the hon. member is probably aware, the port of shipment is a matter for negotiation between the Russian buyers and the milling companies in the case of flour. The government is not directly involved and cannot interfere with the terms of contract. New tenders are being called shortly for flour and it remains to be seen where the point of shipment will be. But I would imagine that each port, particularly Halifax and Saint John, would be competing for this business. Nearly all the traffic to the Caribbean area goes from the port of Halifax, as the hon. member knows; but shipments to the U.S.S.R. and the United Kingdom have been largely made from the port of Saint John, New Brunswick.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)
Speaking of wheat, we anticipate that during the winter months Halifax will have a good shipping season. On the strength of the
November 18, 1966

question asked today, and other observations made, we will look into the situation in the port of Halifax as it affects future shipments.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to raise another subject. This has been raised in committee. I noted that in his opening remarks, the minister mentioned the travel bureau and the tourist industry. It is not necessary to remind the minister and the committee that the tourist industry is one of our largest businesses bringing in foreign currency. Speaking of one particular problem-my remarks may overlap another branch of government-I wish to refer to the Industrial Development Bank, and I hope the minister brings what I say to the attention of the Minister of Finance. When Expo is over we shall still have to rely on a large body of tourist businesses across Canada to maintain our national tourist income. The industry faces money problems. In normal times there is difficulty raising money, because the tourist industry is not classified as highly secure, being in many cases seasonal. The industry has difficulty in raising funds from the private sector and is placing more and more reliance on the government.
When I was first elected to this house in 1957, the tourist industry had nowhere to go for funds. The private sector refused to lend them money, and government agencies also were not lending. In the meantime, there has been progress because the tourist industry is included in the Small Businesses Loans Act. But these loans are only for improvements and are not for refinancing, nor for partial improvements and partial refinancing. The act has helped but it is not exactly what is now needed.
The other source of funds is the Industrial Development Bank. In 1957 the Industrial Development Bank did not consider the tourist business an industry and made no attempt to give it loans. Subsequently, around 1961 the bank revised its policies and now the tourist industry is included in industries receiving loans. The Industrial Development Bank, being a branch of the Bank of Canada, treats itself as a bank. It approaches loans to tourist businesses and to other industries as bankers would in making investments, rather than as a government agency promoting development. This I think is the wrong approach.
From time to time I have heard of many businesses-mostly tourist businesses-which have been restricted so much in the loans they might receive by collateral, security, and hings like that, that they do not get what
Supply-Trade and Commerce they need. In the end, they are worse off than if they had not bothered borrowing money. The complaint I have about the Industrial Development Bank, affects the tourist industry, and I should like the minister responsible for the travel bureau to look into this. I notice that a former minister of northern affairs is present who was responsible for this department at one time.
I hope that the Minister of Finance or some minister responsible will give a policy direction to the Industrial Development Bank to approach loans to tourist businesses in a freer manner, to approach these loans as a government agency promoting industry rather than as a government agency lending money.
Let me show the ridiculous way in which the bank now works. Some businesses, when they want to repay money borrowed in advance of the due date, have to pay a 5 per cent or 6 per cent premium on the money being repaid. In other words, when they want to prepay part of the loan in a good year, they have to pay a 5 per cent premium for the privilege of paying off the money. Then, if they have a bad year, they are in trouble if they cannot meet payments. That is not satisfactory. I hope that the minister considers the interests of the tourist industry, and I think we should do more for that industry now than we have at any time past.
I know of many businesses in my area which are discontinuing this year through lack of funds. I was told of eight or 10 fairly substantial businesses which will not operate next year because they are short of money and cannot refinance. There is nowhere for them to turn. In the private sector, the tourist industry is the last in line. As money becomes tighter, the industry finds money more difficult to obtain.
What holds true for the private sector is true for the Industrial Development Bank which considers its first duty to industry, other than the tourist industry. If we are to have a satisfactory tourist industry, the Industrial Development Bank must approach its task with a more liberal attitude. The bank must develop the idea that it is there to keep the tourist industry going, rather than to get money back when it is due.

I wish to make a few comments and to ask a few questions about the travel bureau. I have always taken an interest in this bureau, but particularly since nine years ago I had some responsibility for it.
I note that the travel branch shows a considerable increase in personnel. I wonder
November 18. 1966

Supply-Trade and Commerce whether this is a temporary increase because of the people who will be needed for the centennial celebrations, Expo and so on, or whether this is a permanent increase. I should like to know where the increased numbers of officers are to be used.
We realize that the great bulk of travellers and visitors to this country come and will continue to come from the United States. As a result of being in many countries in Europe this past summer, it struck me that the Canadian government, through the travel bureau, should be doing more to attract travellers to Canada from that area. Because of increasing affluence and increasing travel going on in Europe at the present time, I think a large market is developing there. We have done a little, but not nearly what we ought to have done to attract travellers. I did not see a single poster in railway stations, airports or in any of the places where you would expect to find them inviting people to Canada. It may be that there are posters in places I did not visit, but I did not see any. I should like to know whether the minister is contemplating an effort to attract European travellers to this country. I understand that recently a promotion office has been opened in Mexico. That is all to the good. Possibly there are other areas in central or South America which might be receptive to a program aimed at increasing the number of visitors to this country.
[DOT] (1:50 p.m.)
We seem to be getting into a discussion of particular matters. Could I ask whether the committee wishes to pass item 1, and then go on to deal with other subjects under specific votes?

I have a few remarks to make on item 1. I welcome this opportunity to make these observations in connection with the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I should like to associate myself with a number of my hon. friends who have congratulated the minister on assuming his new responsibility to report to the House of Commons for the Canadian wheat board. I must say that I am still in favour of placing this important board under the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture. However, it may well be that the minister, with his experience as a businessman, will be able to give the wheat board the kind of direction and assistance it needs.
I would be interested to know whether the minister, in his recent discussions with wheat

board officials in Winnipeg, gave any consideration to complaints about extending the crop year to August 20.
I have heard a number of complaints from my riding about actions taken by the wheat board in this respect. I realize the board is endeavouring to move as much grain as possible into marketing position early in the season. At the same time this imposes hardship on farmers in a number of areas. The end of July, the end of the crop year, is about the time farmers are anticipating what the next year's grain production might be. They make a reasonably good effort to get the grain off the farms and into the elevators. But in some areas, particularly in southeast Saskatchewan, prematurely warm weather this year hastened the maturing of the grain and as a result farmers not only got their grain into deliverable positions but began to harvest the 1966 crop; they marketed this year's crop under the old quota.
In this connection, I should point out that the farmer who farms extensively using modern equipment had a great advantage over other farmers and got his crop in first. In consequence, when the latter were ready to market their crops they found the elevators full. They had to sit back and wait.
There is another problem involved here. Over the years the elevator agents who handle the bulk of this grain, have been accustomed to take their holidays for two weeks in August beginning on July 31. They have done so because normally, these two weeks are the slack season. This year, hundreds of these agents were denied the opportunity of taking a holiday. They manned their elevators until August 20, when they found that this year's crop was being delivered, and as a result they did not get away from the elevators at all.
I received a number of complaints about this, and I am wondering whether the situation was discussed in the course of the minister's recent meetings with the wheat board. Perhaps the minister would give us the bene^ fit of his views. It was the first experience of this kind which many of us have had. I was not able to explain the circumstances to the wheat farmers of my area, and I know that other western members were faced with the same difficulty.
I should like to say something, now, regarding the world wheat agreement. I know the agreement has been extended for one year, until 1967. A few minutes ago my hon. friend from Bow River placed some pertinent facts
November 18. 1966	COMMONS DEBATES	10069
on the record concerning the economic situation of western farmers, the vast majority of whom need to market their grain within a reasonable time and at a reasonable price. We remember what happened in 1965 when the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, who at that time had responsibility for the wheat board, allowed the board to get into a price war with our friends south of the border, the result being a fall of between 14 and 18 cents, in the price per bushel. This was translated into a total loss of some $75 million to the pockets of western Canadian farmers, which bears out the statement I made a few minutes ago when I expressed the hope that the minister would take responsibility for assisting the wheat board in resisting the pressures which are placed upon it at the present time in connection with the continuation of the world wheat agreement.
As far as western farmers are concerned, this is one of the most basic and most important commodity agreements in existence. I realize, in considering this subject, the influence of the policies being followed across the line. Under the policy followed by Mr. Dean Rusk, a great deal is being done to preserve United States leadership in the fight against communism by exporting wheat surpluses on a non-commercial or cut price basis to developing countries, as a humanitarian and political measure. I cannot disagree with this policy. But as a result, there has been a tendency for wheat to sell at prices lower than those which the world wheat agreement would wish to recognize, with consequent pressure on the wheat board. I believe the minister could go to the assistance of the wheat board in a situation such as this. We, as Canadians, cannot afford to have these pressures brought to bear on the grain markets of the world. It should be borne in mind that the United States consumes approximately 85 per cent of its total grain production domestically and need to export only about 15 per cent. In Canada, the opposite is true. We consume only about 15 per cent of our total production and depend on an export market to the extent of 85 per cent.
Obviously, wheat sales and wheat prices are matters of great consequence to western agriculture, and I suggest to the minister that when negotiations for a new world wheat agreement take place he should give every support to the officials of the wheat board and others who will be carrying on the discussions. He should approach these matters on
Supply-Trade and Commerce the basis that a healthy increase in price is desirable.
[DOT] (2:00 p.m.)
He should keep in mind the fact that there should be an increase in the price of wheat. This is the chief saleable commodity, along with livestock, that the western farmer has. There is an ever increasing cost in the goods and services which he requires. It is known that he has to pay anywhere from $8,000 to $12,000, or even a greater price, for a combine or tractor, as compared with half that amount,
10	or 15 years ago. He must not only increase his production, and use all the technical know-how he can obtain, but he must also have better prices for the goods and services he provides. Otherwise, he will have to get out of the agricultural industry due to the cost price squeeze. As I have said the minister has a very important role to play as the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board.
The hon. member for Bow River referred to the oil industry. I come from one of the particularly fortunate areas of Canada which has a large oil development. We have over 6,000 producing wells in the province and about 5,000 of them are in the riding of Moose Mountain. The people engaged in that industry, naturally are very interested in the policy of the present government in respect of the export of oil and oil quotas. Along with many others, I feel that we have a disgracefully low quota at the present time for export of oil from Canada. If the minister has time, I should like to invite him to come to that part of Saskatchewan, particularly the Estevan area, where a great number of the
011	companies in Saskatchewan have their head offices. He could discuss this matter with them and obtain advice. I am sure he would be welcomed by these people and would acquire at first hand information concerning some of the problems in the oil industry and the policies in respect of marketing oil.
I could speak at great length concerning these matters, but I believe my colleague the hon. member for Bow River expressed the position very clearly. I should like in the main, to go along with the suggestions he made concerning the oil industry.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be brief. You or anybody else will be entitled to ring the gong if I go beyond two minutes. First, I should like to thank the minister very warmly for his kind remarks about the excellent port facilities in Halifax. I agree that once a contract is signed it would
November 18. 1966

Supply-Trade and Commerce not be easy for the government to step in and suggest the use of particular facilities in Canada for handling the flour shipments. I think, however, that in the future the minister or his department might point out to prospective purchasers that the government would like to see the wealth shared between the two ports.
In backing the request of the international longshoremen, my final point is to ask the minister whether he and his department would do everything possible to help promote trade through the Atlantic ports. I think there is some uncertainty in the shipping field at the present time. Perhaps this results from the fact we have not passed the railway legislation. I realize that this is more the responsibility of the Minister of Transport, but perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce could urge him to take away any of the uncertainties which exist in the local harbours in the area I represent.

Mr. Chairman, I have only two comments to make with regard to the estimates of this department. Both relate to the Canadian Wheat Board. No doubt the minister is aware that at the present time, under the regulations of the Canadian Wheat Board, permit book holders are required to deliver at a specific shipping point. Several years ago I believe the practice was to give the permit book holder a choice between several delivery points. Certainly, there was more than one point at which he could deliver. Whatever the rationale was for making this change, the persistent feeling now-and I think it is an increasing one-is that the regulation is too restrictive.
At some shipping points, of course, there are a number of elevator companies operating, so the problem is not too great. Other shipping points in the prairies, and certainly in the area which I represent, are located in small towns or villages where there may be only one elevator company operating. In that case the deliverer is, in a sense, captive. Of course he is protected by certain regulations administered by the Board of Grain Commissioners and by the Canadian Wheat Board, but nevertheless it seems to me it is not an unreasonable request that the regulations of the Canadian Wheat Board in this regard be looked at closely with a view to going back to the practice which obtained only a few years ago. If this were done, I think it would meet with the approval of a good number of western grain producers.
The second point I have in mind has to do with the issuance of the initial payment to
{Mr. McCleave.l
grain producers. Of course, this matter has been before the house for some time. Questions have repeatedly been put to the appropriate minister by several members on this side of the house. So far, however, we have received only evasive answers to the effect that the matter is under consideration. Repeatedly, the request has been for an increase in the initial payment. I do not think this is an unreasonable request. At the present time the level stands at $1.50. If it were increased 16 cents or 17 cents per bushel, basis No. 1 at the lakehead, then this still would not put it beyond the floor price of the International Wheat agreement. Therefore it would not be imprudent on the part of the Canadian Wheat Board to accede to this kind of request. If an initial payment increase of 16 to 25 cents does not put the price much beyond the floor prices of the International Wheat agreement, then it cannot be a dangerous thing to do. No one could fault the Canadian Wheat Board if they acceded to this request; it would not be an imprudent policy on their part, I suggest. If the minister has the information readily at hand, I should like to know why there has been this persistent procrastination in respect of finalizing this particular issue.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
The fact is that during the course of the past several months the cost of production to the farmer has surged upward aggravating the situation which has existed for many years, namely, the cost price squeeze. Surely, one of the things that the government and the board can do immediately is the adoption of the request to increase initital payments by between 16 and 25 cents a bushel. In this way, farmers would receive an initial payment at least equal to the floor price of the international wheat agreement.

I have very few remarks to make, Mr. Chairman, but I think I should make them during our consideration of item 1, as a follow-up to the remarks of the hon. member for Moose Mountain regarding wheat deliveries and quotas.
I should like to refer particularly to the interior storage elevator at Moose Jaw. This is a government owned elevator and has a capacity of 5J million bushels. It has not been used to any great extent for the last couple of years. This is a very good elevator situated on the main line of the C.P.R. Some greater use could be made of it in the marketing and handling of grain by the Canadian wheat board. I know this elevator has been equipped
November 18, 1966

for grain deliveries in boxcars. Having made some inquiries I know this elevator could be altered at a cost of a few hundred dollars so grain could be delivered directly by truck. This situation has been brought to the attention of the wheat board, but I hope the minister will look into this matter so this elevator can be used to handle grain delivered by truck, either from farmers under their own wheat delivery permit books or by large trucking companies from country elevators. Then, there would be more room in the country elevators, permitting farmers larger delivery quotas immediately following harvesting operations, and they would not have to store so much grain during the winter or in the following year.
I am sure the minister has received reports about tough and damp wheat. Let me draw to his attention the fact that the Moose Jaw elevator has very modern grain drying facilities. It has a large capacity and could be utilized to put this grain into good condition.
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition referred to the high proportion of high quality wheat grown this year. I understand that the latest contracts with Russia and China are for four and five grade wheat although, as the minister has said, there is a loophole in this regard. I trust that if four and five grade is not available the minister will use every means at his disposal to market this high quality grain at the higher price, so there will be a greater return to the farmer.
The hon. member for Halifax asked questions about flour export. The latest statistical review by the D.B.S. indicates that the export of flour is down. Not only is the export of flour down, but the manufacture of flour for the home market is down.
The minister announced today that he was going to make a greater drive in respect of exports. I hope he will impress upon the newly developing countries the health value of the consumption of bread made from wheat flour. I have on several occasions strenuously objected to diets, and diet fads which do not include bread. I know the minister's department is not concerned with this, but I hope he will assist the flour manufacturing industry by convincing the department responsible for health diet charts that it should emphasize each individual should eat at least three slices of wheat flour bread per day in the interests of health.
I know the minister has been sitting here through the lunch hour. It is to be hoped that
Supply-Trade and Commerce he can get away soon for a lunch which will include some bread.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to use a few moments of the committee's time to bring out one or two points. Let me congratulate the minister on his new position in relation to the Canadian wheat board. I am sure he will do everything within his power to assist the sale of our wheat, and to discover some way of modernizing our transportation system for the movement of grain. He surely must realize we are using the same boxcars to move grain that we used 40 or 50 years ago.
Under item 1, I wish to refer to the price received by farmers for grain. While I know new negotiations are to be undertaken in connection with the international wheat agreement, it seems that the greatest problem facing farmers in western Canada relates to both the initial price of grain and the over-all price received, that is the initial price plus the wheat board payment.
Farmers today are faced with a very difficult cost-price squeeze. The cost of machinery has progressively increased. Today, I believe the index in respect of farm machinery has risen to 180 as compared with 100 in 1949. The price of grain has not risen to the same extent and farmers are in a worse position today than they have been for 20 years because there is no control over the price of machinery. I do not know how this situation can be controlled without getting into labour and union problems.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
As I see it, Mr. Chairman, Canada should strive for a higher price under the international wheat agreement. I know that a great many people today think that the farmer needs a higher initial payment. I would welcome a higher initial payment, but I th'nk this is secondary to the over-all price that we receive for our grain. I am sure that most farmers welcome a cheque from the wheat board in the spring. I point out that this is our own money, but is paid on a deferred basis. One of the best things that can happen to the farming industry is for the farmer to receive a large cheque in the spring.
I suggest that to keep up with the trend of prices at the present time we must strive for an increase of 50 cents a bushel. I do not think this figure is unrealistic, because of the conditions that exist at the present time. I am a farmer who is very much involved in buying equipment and I know that one of the major problems facing the farmer today is trying to
10072	COMMONS DEBATES	November 18, 1966
Supply-Trade and Commerce find the money to pay for the combines and tractors. These are the biggest and most expensive items that he has to purchase. Four or five years ago, the farmer could buy a tractor for $6,000 or $7,000 to do the work that was necessary. The tractor required to do this work today, when the farmer is trying to farm economically, costs anywhere from $10,000 to $12,000. A combine that in 1962 cost $11,000 is selling today for over $15,000. We all realize that in this period of time the price of grain has not changed. As a farmer, and on behalf of farmers, I suggest that this is one of our major problems. Therefore, I emphasize that we should strive for a higher price under the international wheat agreement.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre mentioned the elevator in the city of Moose Jaw. It has been one of my pet beliefs that we have not been making enough use of our internal terminal elevators. The facilities are there to be used. I bel eve two years ago approximately 238,000 bushels were put into that elevator. Last year, I believe approximately 600,000 bushels of No. 6 grain, were put in. But immediately after the end of the crop year they were taken out. I maintain, and I agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre in this respect, that far more use could be made of our elevators.
I believe that in this day and age we should modernize the equipment used for handling grain. Th s principle has been proved in respect of the automobile industry. The railways were trying to haul automobiles across Canada with old fashioned facil ties, and the trucks took away this business completely. We must modernize our equipment. We must obtain modern cars that can haul three or four times the amount of grain that is hauled at the present time. I realize that this matter falls within the jurisdiction of the Min'ster of Transport, but I am dealing with the movement of grain and to that extent it is a responsibility of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I believe we should have box cars that hold 4,000 or 5,000 busheld of grain. We should have trains that are completely grain-carrying, so that they can haul grain to the terminal and immediately come back pick up another load. Then, the terminal elevators would be used more effectively. The argument will probably be put forward that it would cost a great deal of money to instal this equipment to handle the grain, clean it and get it into position.
We are in the age of automation, and I believe that the cost involved in automating

these facilities would be less than those incurred under the present set-up. I shall not take up any more time of the committee, but would emphasize, Mr. Minister, that we must strive for these things in the very near future, namely, the modernization of our grain handling facilities and a higher price under the international wheat agreement.
The only alternative is to impose price control upon the machinery companies. I realize that if such controls were imposed the effect would be felt all the way down the line. We must take a tougher line with the machinery companies, and I realize that when we do this we get into the problem of labour relations and unions.
I believe these problems must be faced and under the conditions that exists today the farmers must obtain a better price for their grain, on one hand, or we must impose strict controls on the price of machinery on the other. If we do not do these things, we will be put out of the grain business completely.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say just a few words on this subject. In rising at this time I would first of all, wish the minister well with his added responsibilities for the Canadian Wheat Board. I hope he will become increasingly interested in this area of his responsibilities and while in Paris next week will try to think about the problems of the western wheat farmer. I suggest that if the minister thinks he needs an adviser from this side of the house to accompany him to Paris, I could perhaps make myself available. Then I could probably bring him up to date on those things in which the western wheat producer is interested, and we could probably come to some agreement on them.
The Minister of Finance, when speaking in Regina to the Saskatchewan wheat pool delegates, suggested that wheat sales to the European market seemed to be under a cloud. I wondered when I read that statement what the minister meant. Perhaps he would clarify this situation by issuing a statement as soon as he has a clear indication of what the problems may be. I hope the minister is not suggesting that we might be priced out of the European wheat market. But whatever the situation is, I wish the minister would look into it and issue a statement as to what the problems may be.
I also hope that the minister will have salesmen in every part of the world trying to obtain new contracts and increase our sales of wheat, because with the new techniques being
November 18, 1966	COMMONS
used to increase the production of wheat we must increase our sales. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will seriously consider putting salesmen in every part of the world so that new contracts can be obtained.
I am also interested in the activities and promotion of Expo '67, increased exports of potash, and so on. However, all these things have been mentioned by previous speakers, and I do not wish to take up any more of the minister's time. I know he has not yet had lunch. I do hope the minister will look into the possibility of increasing wheat sales, and having salesmen situated throughout the world to increase wheat exports in the years ahead.

How does the D.B.S. gather information in regard to crop figures for western Canada? The reason I ask is that its forecast is usually very optimistic but when the figures are revised there is usually quite a drop from the actual production. This does not help the grain trade of western Canada to the extent that the bureau should be helping it.
I know it is only an estimate, but I hope in future the bureau could be more careful. Its forecast should not be too much out of line with actual production, because if it is this tends to be reflected in the price received. As a colleague of mine said a little while ago, we in western Canada feel that the price of grain, particularly considering the wage increases granted within the past few months, is way out of line. The figure he mentioned of 50 cent a bushel for wheat, or at least $2 on the farm, would not be unrealistic.
These optimistic forecasts tend to knock the price down, and the people with whom we negotiate the international wheat agreement get the idea that Canada's granaries are always bulging with surplus grain. The day is coming when this no longer will be true.
Would the hon. member mind if I get that information and provide it for him more specifically than I can at this moment?
I would be very happy with that.

I would like to bring one point to the minister's attention. Is he directly aware of the tremendous responsibility and the cost that is forced on various establishments and companies in trying to provide the information that is constantly sought by various departments? I know the bureau requires essential information, and that this information is of the utmost benefit to many departments of government. But of late representations which I have been receiving on this matter have been increasing in number. They are coming to me from various firms which feel that in some instances the pursuit of this knowledge is taken beyond the bounds of what might be considered reasonable.
A constant barrage of questionnaires is being sent to companies, and the questions on them are very precise and detailed. They require careful analysis of the entire business procedures of a company, and the information cannot be obtained without direct cost to a company.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
DEBATES	November 18, 1966
The complaints that I have received are not directed at the particular cost but at the impression there is a great deal of confusion down here in Ottawa as to the the type of information that is required. In addition there is tremendous duplication by departments which often request the same information.
I am wondering if any attempt has been made to see if all the questions that are sent to companies are necessary, to see if there is a great degree of overlapping in the information that is sought, to see if the information that is from time to time requested is not already available in a department, and to see if something could be done to simplify the whole process. Otherwise, the government should contribute directly to the costs involved in procuring the information.
This is becoming quite a serious matter, especially for smaller industries whose bookkeeping systems and business methods were not set up to make the gathering of such information an easy job. I would like the minister to give consideration to this matter and see if something can be done to alleviate what is actually a hardship on many companies when they are asked to prepare information for the government. The people involved are sincere in their efforts to answer the questions in detail, but they find the burden has increased to such an extent that they believe something must be done about it.

I shall be very glad to look into that, Mr. Chairman. I know from first hand experience how onerous these returns can become, particularly if one does not regard them as necessary, or feels one is contributing information which is not properly the kind of information the government should have. I would ask the hon. member to be good enough to let me know of any instances where duplication of information is requested by various departments, and then I will be very happy to look into them.
I will do that, Mr. Chairman.

I would like to support the statements made by the hon. member for Kent (Ont.), because I would not like the minister to think that is only, an isolated instance. These complaints are coming in to several members. It is certainly true of secondary industries, where the staff to maintain records at the various offices involved are hard pressed to find the time.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
As the hon. member for Kent (Ont.), said, some way should be found either of reducing
November 18, 1966	COMMONS
the amount of information requested or of reimbursing the firms for the time spent in collecting information. I am not sure that that is necessarily a practical suggestion, but it has been made to me and I pass it along. In some instances firms indicate that they spend two and a half to three days a month collecting information for the government, and it is an entirely profitless operation for them. So, I indicate to the minister that this is a problem that exists across the country, and I lend support to the statement made earlier.

Mr. Chairman, 1 want to ask the minister whether the Dominion Bureau of Statistics will become the statistical gathering agency for the Department of Manpower in acquiring information on which to base its manpower policies, or are they going to set up a duplicate system?

I hope it will not be a duplicate system, Mr. Chairman. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics is the instrument of the government for collecting and analysing statistics, but I should like to be more precise in my reply to the hon. member. If he does not mind, I will send him a note or speak to him and provide him with more precise information.

If I may follow that up, I want to urge on the minister the fact that there will be strong support, at least from this section of the house, for the government to extend the scope and personnel of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. We have received complaints that there is inadequate staff and they are unable to do as good a job as they might otherwise be able to accomplish.
Recently, the director of the Swedish ec-nomic commission appeared before the prices committee, and explained that one of the reasons for their great success in drafting both manpower policies and economic forecasting formulae was the fact that they required from business and industry generally even more information than the industries divulged to their shareholders. However, this information was kept highly confidential, and contrary to their expectation there was no real objection to this because industry found that with sounder forecasting they themselves derived greater benefit.
Notwithstanding what the two previous speakers said-and they may have legitimate points-I hope that the minister will seek to expand considerably both the personnel and the areas in which statistics are gathered. Manpower policies are very important and
Supply-Trade and Commerce will be badly incapacitated if information is not gathered which heretofore has been ignored.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support what was said by the hon. member for Kent (Ont.). Many small businesses, service stations and grocery stores are finding it most difficult to fill in the forms which are sent to them. Many of these small businesses have only three or four employees, some of whom have no bookkeeping experience. Many of the forms sent out are complicated, and these people cannot afford to keep up with bookeeping methods. They, therefore, spend a considerable amount of money in completing these forms. I am wondering whether the minister or the department would simplify the forms and assist these people in this way.

Mr. Chairman, I also wish to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kent (Ont.). I represent small business, and I know the nuisance these reports are to people who are engaged in small business. I should like to suggest to the minister that if his department could in some way simplify these forms, as the last speaker suggested, and also consolidate the forms, and send them out at the end of the fiscal year when the information is readily available to these small business people, it would be of considerable assistance. If they are not themselves competent in bookkeeping, they employ an auditor at the end of the year to prepare their books, and all the information is then available.
Although the department may not realize it, their request is causing much extra work to those in small business. With the other provincial reports business has to prepare these days, you almost have to employ someone to make sure you do not get fined for failing to submit these reports. I think this is unfair. Therefore, the suggestion of simplification and consolidation I think is a good one. If the minister would look into it, this would be appreciated by the small businessmen.

I would be glad to do that. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics is well aware of the onerous burden of reporting. We are not alone in this field; provincial governments and others require information, too. Recently, Treasury Board issued the directive that all returns being sought by the federal government must be reported to D.B.S. so that they can determine to what extent there is duplication. We will endeavour to move as far as we can toward simplification as well.

speechtext: The committee will now consider the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
Mr. Chairman, I just wanted to ask the minister if he will make the usual statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my estimates were entered previously, at which time I made a statement. I think the hon. member for Brandon-Souris adjourned the debate.

I can confirm what the minister has stated, Mr. Chairman. Although I did not conclude my reply, as far as I am concerned I am ready to discuss the various items, but I understand that there are one or two others who would like to make a statement on the first item.
May I just apologize to the minister, Mr. Chairman. His estimates were probably begun when I was absent from the chamber, so I apologize to him.

Mr. Chairman, I will be brief because many of the things I have said about parks I have said a number of times during discussion of the estimates. May I say at the outset that I am very happy the committee on northern affairs and national resources will be visiting the parks and that hearings will be held in Jasper and Banff commencing the week of November 30. I trust the minister will have time to join with these members of parliament, so that not only the members of the committee but the minister himself will be able to hear the grievances
[Mr. Winters.!
which will be presented by the citizens of those areas. They have formed themselves into a committee during the last two years which now comprises more than 500 people.
One particular area of complaint with regard to the parks today is that of security of tenure of land. Although I do not intend to spend much time on this, I hope the minister has read a very able brief prepared by Mr. G. H. Steer, Q.C., of Edmonton. He will be one of the witnesses and will present this brief to the committee. I do not intend to say anything about the brief now, because he will be presenting the facts to the committee.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I think some of the misunderstanding which has occurred about the security of land tenure has resulted from the fact people have confused the objectives written into the act with the idea that the parks today have grown into centres which large numbers of tourists come to visit. The three statements about the objectives and purposes of the parks are set out in three statutes which I will quote. They are brief.
In the original act of 1887 it was set out that the parks are for the benefit, advantage and enjoyment of the people of Canada. No person, no matter what side of the fence he is on, will argue with those objectives.
In 1911, the act was changed. The change was with respect to public parks, and as public parks and pleasure grounds, they were to be for the benefit, advantage and enjoyment of the people of Canada. There is not much difference in this act. In 1930, at a time when the resources of western Canada were handed back to the prairie provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta particularly-it is in this way that those provinces obtained their resources of petroleum and natural gas -parks were formed in areas where they could be preserved in their natural state for the advantage and enjoyment of the people of Canada.
In order that these parks may be enjoyed, certain recreational facilities must be built in accordance with the regulations. Nobody finds fault with that. The act, I submit, has had a very narrow interpretation. After all, members of parliament know that though parliament passes statutes, the words of the statutes are subject to interpretation. A legal officer in some department may say that the words mean one thing, but if the words have not been subjected to the judicial test, that does not mean the interpretation is correct. In
November 18, 1966

other words, the interpretation ought to be a judicial interpretation.
Sometimes we have men of vision and imagination who give words a wider meaning than other people lacking that imagination. Perhaps people of narrow imagination interpreted the law as it applies to the parks, and because of that we are having problems.
The 1930 act said that the parks are hereby dedicated to the people of Canada for their benefit, education and enjoyment, subject to the provisions of this act and regulations, and that such parks will be made use of so as to leave them unimpaired for the use of future generations.
People say that Banff is a small park, but in area it is as large as Prince Edward Island. In fact, if you put all the western parks into one area you would find they were as big as the maritime provinces. Since the formation of the parks in 1930, great changes have taken place. Members on both sides of house discussing the trade and commerce estimates talked of one of our great industries, the tourist industry. The tourist industry fits into the objectives of the parks, because the parks are dedicated to the people of Canada, for their benefit. The people of Canada from all parts of the country visit Banff, to see and enjoy the wilderness. Let us get down to brass tacks, they go there to enjoy the animals, the bears, the antelope and deer. If they want to see those animals they must have a place to stay.
A hotel.

You have to have a place-I beg your pardon. I always enjoy the lady minister because she comes to hear me speak, and I know her interest in this subject. She is so interested that she may even take the place of the present minister; that is no disrespect to him. He may move to a more senior portfolio to accommodate the lady minister. I always enjoy her being here, because she always knows when I am to speak about parks, and because her presence gives the necessary touch to anything I might say.
Senator LaMarsh.

Of course, no one knows what the future holds.
Coming back to the parks, the 1930 act said that they are hereby dedicated to the people of Canada for their benefit, education and enjoyment. Since 1930, and I will not clutter up the record with statistics I previously quoted, the tourist industry in the parks has
Supply-Indian Affairs grown until now almost 2 million people a year from Europe, the United States and Canada, visit Banff National Park. They come to enjoy the wilderness, and above all to enjoy a game of golf on the Canadian Pacific golf course. Incidentally, that course now charges so much that few people can afford to play on it.
The point is that in order to make certain the parks are preserved for the orginal objectives of the act, they must be zoned. There ought to be provision for a visitors' centre. The idea was suggested by this side of the house and carried into effect by the other side. In other words, there ought to be provision for hotels, motels, restaurants and things like that, so that when the people come to the parks on a holiday away from the asphalt jungles in which they live year round they can enjoy the wilderness while staying at a comfortable place. Unfortunately, there has been a divergence of opinion about this matter.
Some people have the idea that if you make staying at the park as difficult as possible, if you have few recreational facilities, you will discourage people coming to the park and the wilderness will not be destroyed. Well, Mr. Chairman, the parks were set up for the benefit and advantage of the people, and if you do away with the facilities I have mentioned nobody would be able to get into the parks. As it is there are great areas of parkland in which no man has yet set foot, and which probably will be unexplored for the next 50 years.
Security of tenure of land is extremely important for the man in the tourist business, who is building facilities. To get the capital to build motels, restaurants and a golf course, so that the average man can play golf and not have to pay $10 when he plays alone, $20 when he takes his wife, and $30 if he takes his son, security of tenure is essential. For businessmen to put up hotels where people will not have to pay $30 per night, and top prices for everything else, that security is essential.
The minister may say we have camping grounds. I took photographs of those grounds last year: they are good grounds, but when you have half p mile of cars lining up waiting to get in-
I agree. I have seen that.

The hon. member agrees with that. When you have that situation, it is not good enough. We have had enough propo-ganda from the minister who has called the

November 18, 1966
Supply-Indian Affairs Globe and Mail and other newspapers to say everything is fine.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: May I ask a question.
No. Let me finish because I will outline the facts in a few moments.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Do not quote $10 golf rates, because there are none.
All right. What is the golf rate in Banff, right now?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: I am not talking about Banff.
Then what are you talking about?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: The hon. member was talking about the Banff golf course-

I was talking of the
Canadian Pacific course. If there is another golf course in Banff I want to hear about it. When the hon. member for Qu'Appel le was the minister he suggested that we should have an ordinary golf course established by the department, so that the average man visiting the park could have recreation. I ask the minister this: is it alright for the rich people to play golf, but not the others? Is that the policy?
Let me get back to the point I was making before the minister tried to get me off the rails. I was talking about security of tenure of land.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: The hon. member was right off the rails.

To build the facilities I mentioned, you must have capital. If you have capital, credit, know-how and management you can make a success of your business. But will any mortgage company, insurance company, or even the Industrial Development Bank set up by the government of Canada lend money to those who want to build motels and hotels in Banff, when it is known that there is no security of tenure to land? The answer is no.
What is the consequence of this? My question implies no criticism of Canada Power or the Canadian Pacific. The average man, I am not talking about the big corporation, cannot get capital, because there is no security of tenure in land to build recreational facilities. So, what happens?
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
Canada Power is allowed to go in and build Sunshine. It is a wonderful venture. But if it
is right for Canada Power, and if it is right for the Canadian Pacific Railway, then surely it is right for the average man who has served the tourist trade for 20 or 30 years in the Banff national park to do the same thing?
These things cannot be accomplished, because the people I am speaking of cannot get capital. Nobody will lend them money because there is no security of tenure in the land they hold. Calgary has grown from a city of 70,000 to a city of more than 300,000 because people are willing to lend other people money for development. I am not suggesting the city should develop the park. I am suggesting that the park should be zoned to make it possible for business to serve the tourists who are coming to Banff. The fact that people must line up for half a mile for toilet facilities is a disgrace. They come with camping equipment and find there is no place for them to hook up to sewer and water services. They have had to move camp very often to prevent the camp sites becoming unsanitary places.
What is the reaction of people from the United States, people from the maritime provinces who come to see the beautiful parks in this area? It is not good. I have raised this question before. I know the minister is able to show us a lot of letters praising the parks and the department. Certainly, a lot of people will write good things about Banff National Park and Lake Louise, because we are talking about the most beautiful area in the whole world. People who stay in the Banff hotel or in the Chateau Lake Louise, and who can afford to pay the prices there, naturally write the minister wonderful letters. But I should like to read the letters, if they are still in existence, from people who have found themselves obliged to line up for hours and hours for the simplest services while the government has been content to turn the parks into a playground for the rich, despite the solemn pledge that the parks were to be devoted to the people of Canada for their benefit and education. This is not the definition which hon. gentlemen opposite are following. In far too many cases people who do not possess a big bank roll cannot spend two or three weeks in these parks.
When the parks were set up, there was some land held in fee simple, as the minister knows. All the land owned by the C P.R. is owned in fee simple, with few exceptions. There were other leases of 99 years, there were leases in perpetuity, and there were 42-year leases with 21 year renewal dates. Any of these leases granted by the crown and still in existence are good leases. If the people

November 18, 1966

who have the need for capital and the people who are prepared to advance the capital were prepared to believe that the Queen would keep her word, as expressed through the government of Canada, there would be no difficulty about obtaining money for development. But what happens? Mr. A owns a motel. He has worked for 25 years and he wishes to retire. He decides to sell. He gets a buyer who arranges the financing. The lease goes into the department. He has to wait six months for a reply, and the department finally tells him, "We consent to the lease being transferred but the terms and conditions of the lease will be changed."
Surely, if this country, in the name of the Queen, signs a contract, then that contract should be of such a nature as to warrant belief in it by the individuals concerned? What happens in such a case as I have described? The sale does not go through.
I know of a small operation in respect of which a transfer could not be secured. What happened? They kept the old name. The new man went in to run it and both took part in management on a share basis. It was claimed the property was to be torn down to provide parking facilities. But that was three years ago and I will wager that it will still be there 15 years from now. What is happening is this: the department refuses to measure up to its legal obligation to approve the assignment of these leases.
The minister talks about compensation. Officials in his department say: we will take over your property but compensation will be paid. We all know that today the expropriation laws both in the provinces and under the federal government are a disgrace. When it comes to expropriation, there are no civil rights left.
How does expropriation take place in connection with land held in fee simple in the parks? The authorities file an order in council with the land council office without notice to the owner. He has lost his property. Should he happen to make a search of title, he will find it is no longer his. That is the situation. They believe they can cancel leases by a mere say-so without any due process of law. That is why those three meetings were held last spring and this summer. These meetings were not arranged on any political basis. The people in these parks in Alberta got so desperate that they sought for and obtained a decent and reasonable hearing from the premier of Alberta; it was because they could not get their grievances across to the minister and to his department.

We know how the committee system works in this house-

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Tell me, later, when there will be an opportunity for me to ask a question.

I am sure there will be an opportunity. I know the minister has always taken a keen interest in this subject. One of the great drawbacks of the committee system in the House of Commons is that the government itself controls the committees through its own members. This has always been the case. A minister wishes to get his ideas across, so he finds government members who will agree with the position he takes. Then, before the report of the committee is made public, it is shaped according to the government's wishes. This is not something which happens only under the Liberal government; it happened when the Conservatives were in power. That is why we hear the whips of the parties stand up and say: Mr. A will cease to serve on a particular committee and Mr. B will serve in his place. They want to make sure that the minister will get his views across in committee.
I must congratulate the present minister, who I see is smiling in his place. When I hit him intellectually, he always enjoys it.
Impossible.

I would not say that. I have not seen any changes in the committee on northern affairs and national resources, and I hope when that committee goes out west it will do so with an open mind and listen to a man like Mr. George Steer, Q.C. So that there may not be any misunderstanding, let .me say that Mr. Steer is one of our leading counsel and that he has been before the judicial committee of the privy council as many times as most lawyers have appeared in their trial courts.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
Intellectually he is an honest man and, I understand, he is a Liberal by politics. So, I am quite sure when he presents his point of view it will be presented on a factual and legal basis. There will be no prejudice. The minister will not be able to say that the man is prejudiced, because even in his political philosophy he is on the same side of the fence as the minister. Five hundred people were at this meeting at Banff and Jasper. There were 500 of them, and the minister would not attend that meeting. He refused to go to the meeting.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:

That is what it says in the letter. If it is wrong, I will take the minister's word. He was not there. He should have been there. Senator Cameron said that he should have been there. I say he should have been there. The chairman of the Banff council said he should have been there, and he was not there. I say this nicely, but I think the reason you were not there was that you were afraid to be there because the grievances were so great and you were so wrong. You could not stand up before such a group.
I hope that this committee will go out there and that the members of the committee will have open minds. I hope that the report which will be written will rise above politics so that these people who are serving the tourist trade will get a fair shake. I believe in the objectives concerning the national parks. Rezone the national parks for recreational centres. The zones can be small in size; they can be in areas other than Banff and Lake Louise. However, let us have the facilities which are required by the people who are serving the tourists. Let them have security of tenure of land so that they can obtain the kind of capital which is necessary to build the required enterprises which should be built at Banff.
We have had some tremendous people in this department. It have not always agreed with Mr. Coleman, but I will say that he is a dedicated civil servant. He has done a tremendous job in the parks. I would be the first to make that statement. But, when we come to this kind of policy within the department I cannot agree with it. I am not attacking you, sir, personally, but I am attacking something which has been gross in the sense that nothing has been done about it. Immediately, the minister will get up and say that the Conservative government passed a certain order in council in 1958 which started this trend.
I was not the minister at that time, but I can tell you that these problems existed then and I was fighting them as strongly as I am now. I see the former minister in the house. When I went to him, he and his executive officials sat down with me and ironed out the problems.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Is that so?

It is so, and it was not that order in council of 1958 which started this trend. Even if it did, let us take your side of the argument. If it was wrong in 1958, let us not perpetuate it in 1966. What kind of political nonsense is it to say, "Sure, the problem is terrible, but you Tories started it". I am not

admitting we did start it. Often a minister becomes a prisoner in his own department. I do not think our minister ever was, but I am afraid that this is what happened to you. I do see some tremendous changes, however, and I hope you will go out with the committee to Banff. We know that it is not an easy task to administer the parks. We know that some people like to have monopolies. It may be that in these cases the minister has a very difficult problem. It is very difficult because there always are political overtones when one is dealing with the people who are in the parks. It may be easier for a member in the opposition to represent the parks than it is for a member on the government side. Perhaps that is a truism.
Let us not have the kind of nonsense where say, "Because you started something therefore I am going ahead with it". Let us take a realistic approach. These people have been denied their just rights. I am not suggesting I believe that people in Calgary or some place else should be allowed to build houses in the parks. But I do say that these people should be allowed to build adequately in order to serve the tourist industry, which is the second industry of Canada. The Premier of Alberta backs this stand. The minister of economics in Alberta backs this stand, and I back it. I think that anyone who has done any research in this regard cannot help but come to the same conclusion. Surely, this committee will take a real look at it. I will do my part. I will try to remain as polite as possible, and say I hope you will give those witnesses a real hearing and come to a proper judgment on the evidence rather than on some pre-conceived idea that you are going to do something whether they like it or not. I do not say the minister is taking that attitude, but that attitude has been indicated to certain people.
If you are short of staff in the department, for goodness sake at least get some people to answer the mail. Wherever I have gone in Jasper, the grievance has been that no replies were received.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: That is not correct.

That is correct. I can read from the report of the committee. Your deputy minister said that he would look into it. I have a letter of apology. Do not shake your head; that does not make something right that is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
You are making a generalization out of a single case. You should not do that.
November 18, 1966

At that meeting which you would not attend, numbers of people got up complaining they did not get answers to their letters. Senator Cameron will back me up on this. He, himself, could not get answers to his letters.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: He got some answers that he did not want.

He also got some answers that he did like, because he still fought for the people of Banff. Surely, this is an important grievance which the minister should not take as just another political knock. I hope that I will receive support from some other Alberta members. I see that the hon. member for Medicine Hat, who usually is in his seat, has just gone out.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: He could not stand you.

speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but the time allotted his speech has expired.
I just wish to say one thing to the minister. He does not believe that.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Will you answer a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has made a great to-do over the sanctity of contracts for all time. I should like to ask him whether he will tell me, now that he would insist upon a contract for eternity, why a lessee is paying the government of Canada $7 per year, receiving all the services for that $7 a year, and building thereon a $60,000 summer home for him and his family when the government which he supported in 1958 decided that it simply was not possible to extend that sort of a privilege to people in Canada?

I should like to answer this fully and honestly. You have taken the example of a home. In this argument I pointed out that I did not go along with the idea of people having summer homes. I know that Mayor MacKay, one of the biggest Liberals, built a summer home. I could name other persons who did this through monopolies. There may be some on this side of the house who have built homes, but they are wrong. I do not wish to mention the names of any motels, but people have begged for the opportunity to extend their enterprises. They are good operators. The minister knows who I mean. Some
Supply-Indian Affairs of them are around Lake Louise and Banff. They have been told they cannot extend their enterprises unless they accept a new term. If the rent is $7 a year or $7 a month, then tax them in accordance with their capital return and you will not hear a squeal.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The way it is they do not have the security of tenure of land. In the cities, where we operate on titles, if the taxes are not high enough the authorities do not take over the whole house, they just increase the rate of tax.
Let us not be nonsensical and refer to one individual who had a summer home. I hope the minister does not make the same mistake made by Maclean's when it took a picture of a run-down restaurant outside the park at Canmore and played it up as though it was part of the park. That is the same error you are falling into now. This picture was of a terribly rundown place and the suggestion was that this was in Banff national park. Everybody in Ontario who read that article believed that was the situation, but it was completely misleading.

I rise at this time to say a few words about the wildlife program of the department of national resources which, since I have been in this House of Commons, has received very little publicity or backing. At this time in all fairness, and I think even the opposition members will agree with me, I congratulate the minister and his department for their forward-looking park policy. The policy followed by the administrators of our national parks has a great deal to do with the preservation of our wildlife, and it is essential that a strict protective policy be adhered to.
I agree with the hon. member for Bow River who said practically the same thing I now intend to say. Any park policy has to be a policy for the people. Space for family camping, tourism and recreation have to be given utmost consideration by our park administrators. I am sure we all agree with the minister and his department that consideration for the wildlife angle, with its cultural, scientific, educational and inspirational aspects, must be given.
Today, with more spare time on people's hands and with more money in their pockets, we are faced with an ever increasing demand for outdoor recreation. That is true in spite of the claims of the wheat growers across this country that they are facing the worst time in history. I should like to know how so many of them are able to go south this year in their Cadillacs.
It is heartening to note that the department is already doing something about this situation through park zoning. I understand the department has a park zoning program under consideration and has taken steps for the establishment of an appropriate review authority to inquire into outdoor recreation requirements not only for our immediate requirements, but for those over the next 30 or 40 years.
November 18, 1966

In today's atmosphere of big business, outer space, and so on, I wonder whether we as Canadians are really aware of the treasure that is our wildlife heritage? This is a heritage that goes back to the first explorers, trappers, fur traders and homesteaders when wildlife often meant the difference between survival and starvation.
With the advancement of civilization, we have drained the wetlands, burned the vegetation, taken off the top soil, cut the timber and we have strewn chemical poisons by planes and thus dumped them into our rivers and lakes. Do not tell me there has not been a change in our wildlife habitat. There is no doubt about that and, therefore, it is a good thing that provincial and federal governments have finally recruited highly trained scientists to probe to the fullest the effects these changes have had, and to devise methods of managing wildlife in an effort to offset these changes. These people are moving forward.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I would like to point out at this time that Canada is very, and I emphasize "very", short of trained scientists to carry on this work. I feel that a special effort to remedy this situation should be made by government and, yes, also by industry which has become wealthy by acquiring and harvesting these natural resources. I am referring to the lumbering industry, the pulp and paper industry and the mining industry. I understand that some money, though not a very great amount, has been allotted by the government and a few companies for wildlife scholarships. However, more has to be done in this respect. This is one practical way, I think hon. members will agree, to interest our young students to expend their efforts in this field.
I wonder whether hon. members realize that it has been estimated that during the next ten years 160 professionals and 545 technicians will be required in the park management field just to fill the vacancies that will exist without allowing for any expansion. Therefore I do feel most sincerely that more consideration has to be given by the government to increasing these scholarships. Private enterprise, those industries that I mentioned, should be approached, and if necessary pressure should be put on them to contribute to these scholarships.
The trouble is that when a great many people think of wildlife-this applies especially to sportsmen-they naturally think of hunting and fishing. And what experience can be greater if these activities are carried on on the proper scale? However, as I have already
Supply-Indian Affairs mentioned, the economics of hunting have changed greatly along with the environment that I mentioned previously.
The January 15,	1966, edition, of the
Financial Post ran a full page story on hunting and what it means in dollars and cents. I have often wondered whether we think of what hunting means to this country in dollars and cents. I am not always interested in what these things mean in dollars and cents, but I should like the committee to know that some 790,000 hunters spent $88 million on their sport in 1961. They travelled 245 million miles by car, 4 million miles by privately owned boats, and over 16 million miles by train, aircraft and other means of transportation. The Financial Post estimated that a conservative total of the amount spent in 1964 on hunting was $118 million, and this figure is rising steadily. Probably this year it is up to $130 million.
Let us not forget that these figures refer to pleasure hunting only, not hunting for food. We often say that people hunt for food, but in the great majority of cases this is not so. But let us as Canadians not forget that there are many people in Canada who rely directly on game for their livelihood and even for their very existence. Fur trapping is still an important occupation in Canada. In 1962-63 the sale of Canadian wildlife furs totalled more than $12.1 million. Many of our Eskimos and Indians earn their livelihood from fur trapping and they need wildlife for food and clothing. One could say a great deal on that subject alone.
Of course, wild animals also help to control insects, birds and small mammals which damage crops; in other words, the control exercised by wildlife helps to keep these things in balance. However, the main objective of Canadians concerned with the future of wildlife is that it should be managed properly as a renewable natural resource of great value. Yes, above all else, Mr. Chairman, wildlife management in Canada must place stress on the preservation of the natural habitat as much as on the preservation of the birds, mammals and fish which live therein. A wild bird or animal and its surroundings cannot be separated. We all know it is true that one cannot be preserved without preserving the other.
It is therefore most reassuring to the Canadian public, and wildlife enthusiasts in particular, to learn of the new federal migratory bird program whereby it is proposed -listen to this; this is what the department of northern affairs is doing and it is

November 18, 1986
Supply-Indian Affairs a forward step that has never been taken by this department in any other government-to lease some five million small potholes on the prairies. Why is this being done? It is to prevent their destruction by draining or filling. Pilot projects have been carried on for three years in order to work out administrative and legal techniques. This is to be a ten-year program starting in 1967, and under the program $5 million will be spent annually. In other words, in the next ten years the department of northern affairs will spend some $50 million to prevent the destruction of wildlife breeding grounds.
I have been talking only about potholes on the prairies, but additional expenditures on behalf of migratory birds will be necessary for the preservation, by purchase or long-term lease, of large marshes not only on the prairies but elsewhere in Canada. The marshes that are going to be leased or bought are important as breeding, resting and over-wintering areas. I believe this is one of the most important projects that any government has taken in sustaining and protecting wildlife.
Apart from this program-and many opposition members know this is true-because of the unending perseverance of the minister of northern development, and I know the perseverance he has shown, the new Canadian migratory game bird permit came into being by government order in council. I know how hard the minister worked privately to bring this into being. It was not an easy thing, let me tell hon. members.
To sportsmen this permit is known as the duck stamp, and it will pay a very important role in estimates of kill by species and location. This is a big step forward, because without these estimates it would be a little 1 ke management endeavouring to operate a business whose volume and distribution of sales were unknown. In other words, the department is taking a very forward-looking step in respect of wildlife management. I personally would like to congratulate the minister and his department for taking this step, and I know I speak on behalf of every member of this house and the sportsmen of Canada.
